title: A transform is only as good as its inverse: reading the cost of power, log, quantile, tanh and polar maps
summary: Each of these course animations applies a one-line transform to data or to a grid and then prints what it costs: error amplification of a power map, the plateau of a log scale, a heavy tail against normal quantiles, round-off at the saturated end of tanh, the jump of an angle chart, the local stretch of a conformal map. Companion static figures add the slope of the power map at the origin, a clamp against an additive epsilon, the Box-Cox slope, float64 round-trip errors, a branch cut, and four curvilinear grids.

media.alt: Four stills side by side. Left: a power curve z equal x to the power p against the line z equal x, and a decreasing curve of inverse amplification against p. Others in the group show decay curves on a log time axis, an empirical distribution against normal quantiles, a histogram piled at plus and minus one with a round-trip error curve, an angle that jumps by two pi, and a bent polar grid.

read_the_figure.question: What does this transform do to the quantity I care about, and how much error, range or structure does it cost when I undo it?
read_the_figure.axes: Each still has one to four panels with its own axes; most are log in the vertical or horizontal direction. Panel titles carry the numbers: for example p = 1.58, eps = 8e-06 with plateau spread 0.801, scale s = 1.3, a 0.38 parameter on the conformal grid.
look_at: S004: the left panel is z = x^p against the dashed identity line; the marked point x = 1 has slope p. The right panel plots how an assumed 2 percent error in z becomes a relative error in x: about 1/p of it.
S005: three decays with rates 1, 100 and 10000 in raw space and after log(y + eps). The title's spread (0.801) measures how far apart the plateaus sit.
S006: the empirical distribution of 121 values and a quantile plot against normal quantiles; a curve bending upward at the right is a heavy right tail.
S007: a histogram of tanh(x) piled against -1 and +1, and a round-trip error that grows with the scale.
S008 and S009: an angle that jumps at the cut, and a grid mapped by a conformal map with two printed numbers, the orthogonality deviation (about 1e-8 degrees) and the stretch ratio max|F'|/min|F'|.

Companion figures. Power-map slope: the tangent of the sign-power map near the origin as the exponent p changes, shown at three small x; only p = 1 gives a finite, nonzero slope as x goes to 0, so only p = 1 is a diffeomorphism at the origin.
Clamp against additive epsilon: near y = 0 the clamped log is flat below epsilon (zero derivative, so no gradient) while the log of y + epsilon is smooth through zero.
Box-Cox slope: the value stays finite as x goes to 0 for lambda below 1, but the slope x^(lambda-1) diverges, on a log-log plot a straight line of slope lambda - 1.

Float64 round trip: errors of atanh(tanh x) grow rapidly with x and the map saturates (tanh at x about 19, the sigmoid at about 37); a second panel shows the arcsine flat-tangent regime where the round-trip error equals the perturbation below a crossover near 1e-8.

Angle field: the angle atan2(y, x) in a cyclic colour map with the branch cut drawn; going once around the origin changes the angle by 2 pi, so no continuous angle function exists on the punctured plane.

Four grids: confocal elliptic, parabolic, bipolar and toroidal (a meridian slice) coordinate lines, with the places where the Jacobian vanishes marked (foci, a segment, an axis). The 3D toroidal figure shows nested tori shrinking onto a focal ring, with |det| going to zero at both ends of the toroidal parameter.
read_the_figure.proves: The printed numbers show whether the transform is safe for the job: error amplification below 1 or above 1, a plateau that hides small values, a saturated end that cannot be inverted, a cut that makes a smooth quantity discontinuous, a stretch that is local and not uniform.
if_wrong: A critical point of the power map at 0 (slope 0 there): the inverse blows up and small z errors become large x errors.
A log scale with too small an epsilon: tiny values dominate the range; too large: the structure is flattened.
A saturated end of tanh: values near plus or minus one lose digits and can round to exactly one, so the inverse returns infinity.
An angle chart used across its cut: a model sees a jump of 2 pi in a quantity that is physically continuous.
must_check: That the inverse is tested, not just the forward map.
That a log-type map states its offset epsilon.
That a bounded map (tanh) reports how close data come to its bound.
That a chart states where its cut is.
That each number printed in a title is read at the point of the animation you are looking at: it changes as the animation plays.

terms.meaning: z = x^p. Relative errors in z become relative errors in x divided by p.
The factor by which a small error in the transformed variable is multiplied when mapped back.
z = log(y + eps). It makes multiplicative differences additive and spreads quantities over many decades.
The fraction of data not exceeding x. Used as a quantile transform to make data uniform.
Sorted data against the matching quantiles of a normal distribution. A straight line means normal.
A map that flattens toward a bound, for example tanh near +-1.
A coordinate system valid except on a cut. The polar angle jumps by 2 pi across its cut.
A map that preserves angles but may change scale from point to point.

remember: For z = x^p the relative error of x is the relative error of z divided by p.
A log transform turns y = exp(-kt) into a straight line of slope -k; epsilon sets where the line stops.
tanh has derivative 1 - tanh^2, which vanishes at the ends: its inverse amplifies errors there.
A quantile transform erases magnitude information; keep the table that undoes it.
A conformal map keeps right angles right but not lengths.

steps.title: Error amplification of a power map
steps.note: Take logs of z = x^p and differentiate. The right panel of the first still plots the factor 1/p; for p above 1 the inverse shrinks relative error, for p below 1 it enlarges it.

steps.title: Why a log scaler spreads decays
steps.note: Each rate becomes a straight line until y falls to about epsilon, then all lines flatten at ln(eps). The plateau spread in the title measures how much of the range the unflattened part occupies.

steps.title: The saturated end of tanh
steps.note: A fixed rounding error in y (about 1e-16 in double precision) becomes an error cosh^2 x times larger in x, which grows fast. That is the rising orange curve in the round-trip panel.

steps.title: Quantile transform to uniform
steps.note: Sorting turns any one-dimensional data into a uniform variable; the inverse is a table lookup. A heavy tail in the raw quantile plot is squeezed into the last few percent of u.

steps.title: The jump of an angle chart
steps.note: A smooth path through the cut shows a jump of 2 pi in phi. The value jumps, the geometry does not: the cure is another chart, or the pair (cos phi, sin phi).

steps.title: Conformality from the complex derivative
steps.note: The Jacobian is a rotation times a scale |F'|, so angles survive. Where |F'| varies, a square grid cell becomes a curved cell of different size; the ratio max|F'|/min|F'| measures how much.

steps.title: Slope of the Box-Cox map
steps.note: The value z stays finite at x = 0 for positive lambda, but a map with an infinite slope amplifies small errors without bound near zero: the straight lines of the companion figure on log axes have slope lambda - 1.

steps.title: Round trip through a saturating map
steps.note: With a rounding error of about 1e-16 in y, the recovered x has error about 1e-16 times cosh^2 x; the tanh figure's error curve climbs to order one near x of about 19 where tanh x rounds to exactly 1.

worked.title: A 2 percent error in z through p = 1.58
worked.problem: The power-map still sets p = 1.58 and an assumed 2 percent error in z. What relative error in x do you get?
worked.answer: About 1.3 percent, which agrees with the marked point on the right panel (just above 1e-2 on its log axis).

analyze.q: For a log scaler with a tiny epsilon, which of the three raw decays (k = 1, 100, 10000) ends up with the largest share of the transformed range, and why is that a problem for a loss?
analyze.hint: Straight lines in log space continue until y reaches epsilon.

analyze.q: The tanh histogram is piled at +-1. What does that say about the scale s relative to the data, and which two numbers would you print in the title?
analyze.hint: Saturation fraction and the round-trip error.

analyze.q: On the angle chart a model is trained on phi. Describe two fixes and what each costs.
analyze.hint: Move the cut; or use a pair of smooth coordinates.

evaluate.q: Rank the transforms in this group by how safe their inverse is for use inside a trained pipeline, and justify with the printed numbers.
evaluate.hint: Amplification, saturation, loss of magnitude information.

evaluate.q: Is the conformal stretch ratio a reason to reject the map, or a quantity to carry through the loss?
evaluate.hint: The Jacobian is known analytically here.

create: Design a single title line, in the style of these animations, that would let a reader of a log-scaler figure decide on epsilon without opening the code.
Propose a transform for a quantity that is positive, spans eight decades and has a hard upper bound, and say what you would print to certify its inverse.

checks.q: Why does p above 1 shrink relative error in x?
checks.hint: Relative error of x is relative error of z divided by p.
checks.answer: Because dx/x = (dz/z)/p: the power map stretches relative changes by p on the way in, so undoing it divides the error by p.

checks.q: A relative error of 3 percent in z, p = 3. Relative error in x?
Why does the round-trip error of tanh rise with the scale?
checks.hint: Which factor in dx/dy grows near the bound?
checks.answer: Larger scale pushes more values toward +-1 where 1/(1-y^2) = cosh^2 x is large, so rounding in y becomes a large error in x, and eventually y rounds to exactly 1 and the inverse is infinite.

checks.q: Is a quantile transform a good normalizer for a physical field you must later map back?
checks.answer: Only if you keep the sorted table. It discards the magnitudes of gaps, is flat between data points, and cannot extrapolate outside the training range, so it is a poor choice if the inverse must be accurate beyond the data.

checks.q: Give a smooth replacement for the angle phi that has no cut.
checks.answer: The pair (cos phi, sin phi), or a unit vector, is continuous around the full circle; the price is one extra coordinate and a constraint.
